scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Logobi appeared in Côte d'Ivoire in the 1980s (specifically traced to 1986), spreading across the working-class ghettos of Abidjan, particularly Abobo, as well as university campuses.
It grew out of the loubard (street gang) subculture.

Urban lore and diaspora accounts credit John Pololo (Sahiri Gnédré Lazare, 1962–2000), a martial artist and leader of the gang 'Vagabons Sauvés' (VS), as its inventor and codifier who fused martial arts movements with street music.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Derived from the Nouchi concept of getting by through cunning and street smarts, the dance communicates the social realities of poverty, misery, and street struggle while voicing hope for prosperity, peace, and justice.
It serves as both street bravado and social expression.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is characterized by rapid, highly expressive arm maneuvers—giving it the nickname 'la danse des gros bras'—alongside jerky, staccato footwork.
Dancers improvise movements inspired by street combat, martial arts punches, secret gang signals, weapon handling, and sexual gestures.
Performances range from spontaneous maquis and block party circles in Côte d'Ivoire to competitive crew battles held in public transit stations.
Watch for Les Gros Bras, Jeux de Jambes Saccadés, Mime de Combat.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Logobi is danced to fast-tempo music with high rhythmic speed.
Musical accompaniments include zouglou rhythms, fast-paced coupé-décalé instrumentals, and heavily compressed electronic beats.
Listen for the synthesizers, electronic drum machines, digital samplers, percussion.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 140 beats a minute.

A high-velocity sonic assault driven by digital kick drums, snappy snare syncopations, and repetitive synthesizer riffs. In its traditional form it relies on heavy Ivorian percussive grooves, while modern diaspora iterations layer buzzy electro synths and hard-tech compression.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Historically practiced in the street environments, maquis (open-air restaurants/bars), and university campuses of Abidjan, it requires no formal ceremonial dress.
In its French diaspora phase, it took place in train stations, subways, and shopping malls among street crews dressed in contemporary urban wear.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures include John Pololo (Sahiri Gnédré Lazare), who codified the dance; musical groups and artists such as Logobi GT, Les Youlés, Yang Systeme, Les Mantanien, Samo Samo, Les Garagistes, Espoir 2000, Magic System, Petit Yodé and l'Enfant Siro, Molière, Petit Denis, Gor la Montagne, and Moussier Tombola; and visual artist Christelle Oyiri (CrystallMess), who documented the Parisian movement.
The original Ivorian variant is grounded in loubard street culture, zouglou, and raw martial arts pantomime.
Logobi evolved out of traditional Ivorian zouglou dance and loubard martial culture during the 1980s.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: logobi is parent of zouglou: Logobi developed directly out of zouglou on Abidjan university campuses, adding martial and street elements.
logobi is influence of coupé-décalé: Logobi preceded and influenced coupé-décalé, which later provided the fast electronic instrumentals often used to dance logobi.
logobi is influence of tecktonik: Logobi absorbed tecktonik and electro elements during its diaspora evolution in the Parisian banlieues.

scenes.title: Step A — slowly
narration: Step 1: Stance: Adopt a balanced, grounded street posture with knees slightly bent and core braced for rapid weight shifts.
Step 2: Gros Bras Pump: Drive clenched fists or open palms out in rapid forward and crossing thrusts, mimicking boxing strikes and martial arts blocks.
Footwork from the sources: Saccadic, jerky steps and rapid weight transfers under a stable center of gravity.
Drill: Find a wide, grounded squat with elbows tucked and fists guarded.
on_screen: Instructor front view, then back view (student's perspective); repetitions per step: about 4

scenes.title: Step B — the next layer
narration: Step 3: Jerky Footwork (Jeux de jambes): Step in quick, staccato, syncopated pulses, snapping the feet under the hips to match high-tempo electronic or coupé-décalé beats.
Step 4: Combat Mime: Integrate stylized street-gang gestures, including defensive parries, simulated weapon draws, and defiant hand signals.
Drill: Pulse in half-time to a fast coupé-décalé beat, keeping heels mobile.
on_screen: Instructor front and back view; slow, then half tempo

scenes.title: Put it together
narration: Step A, then Step B, without stopping. Slow first.
Now half tempo. Now full tempo.
Mirror: the instructor faces you and mirrors, so your right is your right.
Drill: Shift weight side-to-side without elevating head height.
on_screen: Split screen: front view / back view
Tempo label changes: slow → half → full
